transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-18
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (GlobalPay Head of ML), Oliver Price (Platform Engineer), Priya Nair (Sec/Compliance)

Summary: Quick discovery to understand GlobalPay's model needs across multilingual support, long context threads (billing/customer conversations up to 40k tokens), and whether hosted/dedicated/private is the right path. SE to run dedicated perf check and security pack to be shared.

Topics: model selection (open models), context length requirements (8k vs 32k vs 64k), multilingual quality (Hindi/Spanish/Portuguese), tool/function calling (ticketing systems, payments instrument lookup), deployment mode tradeoffs (hosted vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC), SOC2 and KMS concerns.

[00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:05] Maya Singh: Maya here, hi.
[00:06] Oliver Price: Oliver.
[00:07] Priya Nair: Priya here.
[00:09] Ethan Cho: Ethan from Redwood, SE on latency and throughput.
[00:12] Sofia Martinez: Great. Today we're mostly trying to understand your usage patterns, the types of models you want to evaluate (open models vs managed), and any hard constraints on context length or compliance. Maya, can you kick us off with current pain points?
[00:25] Maya Singh: Yeah. So our main thing is customer support summarization and dispute resolution across multiple countries. So we get long threads, sometimes up to 30 to 40k tokens in a single case — like multi-message chat, attachments summarized. We also need decent quality in Hindi and Spanish, and we want to call out to internal systems: order lookup, payment history, and open tickets.
[00:45] Oliver Price: To add, from infra side we care about cost predictability. We currently run an internal LLM that we finetuned but it's getting expensive at scale. We want to compare hosted options versus reserving capacity. Also need to know if Redwood can do function/tool-calling patterns without a lot of glue code.
[01:05] Priya Nair: And security — we need SOC2, SSO integration, KMS for keys, audit logs. Also data residency question for EU customers.
[01:15] Sofia Martinez: Great, thanks. On the model side, are you focused on the very latest research SOTAs, or are you okay with slightly older open models if cost and latency are better?
[01:25] Maya Singh: We want the best customer-facing quality but cost matters. If an open LLM like Llama-3-ish quality with 32k context works vs a much more expensive managed option, that's interesting. Also we care about tool-calling reliability — like consistent structured JSON back from function calls.
[01:40] Ethan Cho: Good notes. High-level, Redwood Hosted gives fastest start — you can hit our API with curated open models (we maintain perf profiles). Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools (predictable throughput) and can run longer contexts with tuned kernels; Private means your control plane sits in your VPC or on-prem with stronger isolation and KMS/HSM integration. For the 30-40k token cases we usually recommend either quantized long-context variants or model sharding with routing to variants; but Dedicated or Private makes sense for predictable latency at that length.
[02:10] Maya Singh: When you say "curated open models" which families do you support? We're looking at Mistral, Falcon, LLaMA derivatives, and some region-specific models. Also is 64k context realistic?
[02:22] Ethan Cho: We have Llama-2/3 derivatives, Mistral mixes, Falcon variants, and other community LMs. For 64k, it's possible but you hit memory and kernel limits depending on quantization and batch concurrency. We can push 64k for single inference on Dedicated with memory-optimized configs but that's a tradeoff with throughput. 32k is the practical sweet spot for many customers.
[02:45] Oliver Price: How do you measure cost for long contexts? Is it per-token only or extra overhead?
[02:50] Sofia Martinez: Our billing is token-based for Hosted; for Dedicated it's reserved capacity plus an overage or unit pricing for burst. We also show token-level cost breakdown in the Console. For 30-40k contexts, we recommend KV prefix caching and chunking to avoid re-encoding the whole history every time.
[03:08] Maya Singh: KV what?
[03:10] Ethan Cho: KV cache — key/value cache, sometimes transcribed in logs as KV cash — it keeps the past KVs per session so repeated tokens don't get recomputed and helps latency. But cache warm-up and TTL need to be tuned.
[03:22] Priya Nair: For Private deployment — does Redwood offer an air-gapped package? We have workflows that may require that for some EU banking partners.
[03:30] Ethan Cho: Yes, we offer Private with options for on-prem and air-gapped installs. There's a private control plane that can be customer-managed; we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. There is an extra compliance and deployment workstream that we handle via our Enterprise Sales/Eng team.
[03:45] Maya Singh: On multilingual — do you have benchmarks for Hindi/Spanish? We don't trust English-only evals.
[03:50] Sofia Martinez: We do per-model multilingual evals but we'll need your domain prompts to get a true picture. We'll share a model perf matrix showing BLEU/ROUGE-type metrics and some human-rated comparisons for Hindi/Spanish.
[04:05] Oliver Price: About tool-calling — can Redwood's function calling support arbitrary webhook calls or is it limited? We want to call our payment microservice to fetch masked PAN and then redact after.
[04:18] Ethan Cho: We support structured function/tool calling patterns via the API where the model returns JSON that we can validate; we have connectors for common services and a generic HTTP action model. For sensitive data, we recommend tokenization and using a sidecar for the actual PAN retrieval; Redwood can orchestrate the call but we don't persist the sensitive payload if you configure the route as non-persistent.
[04:40] Maya Singh: Great. Any limitations around streaming vs function calls? We need low-latency streaming for live agent assist.
[04:48] Ethan Cho: Streaming works with function calls but you have to be aware that until the model emits the function signal, you won't have the structured output. For agent assist we usually stream partial completions and then do a follow-up structured call. It's a little bit of engineering but we provide patterns and SDK helpers.
[05:05] Priya Nair: Coming back to compliance — do you have SOC2 report and do you allow log redaction?
[05:12] Sofia Martinez: Yes we are SOC2 compliant; we'll share the SOC2 type II report in the security pack. Logs can be configured for retention and redaction — and in Private you control logs entirely.
[05:20] Maya Singh: We're leaning towards a pilot. What would you recommend as an experiment to evaluate both quality and system-level metrics?
[05:28] Ethan Cho: Short answer: run a 2-week pilot with Redwood Dedicated. We run a benchmarking window where we bring up dedicated nodes matching your throughput, run your multilingual and long-context prompts, and measure latency tail percentiles, token cost, and success rate for tool calls.
[05:40] Oliver Price: Sounds good. How invasive is the Dedicated spin-up?
[05:44] Ethan Cho: It's mostly configuration and capacity planning. We provision reserved pools and tune the runtime kernels for the model/context combo. There's some networking setup for VPC peering if needed.
[05:52] Maya Singh: Do you support quantized weights and 8-bit/4-bit runs to reduce memory?
[05:56] Ethan Cho: Yes. We use quantized execution paths; some models quantize better than others. We'll include recommended quantization and kernel settings in the perf matrix.
[06:06] Priya Nair: For data residency — can routes be pinned to eu-west regions?
[06:10] Sofia Martinez: Yes. For Hosted we have regional endpoints. For Dedicated/Private you can pin to EU regions and we can discuss network egress policies.
[06:18] Maya Singh: One practical question: our threads sometimes include attachments. Can Redwood pass attachment embeddings or must we pre-embed?
[06:26] Ethan Cho: You can pre-embed attachments and pass them as context vectors or use Redwood embeddings endpoint; we also support multi-modal inputs in some model variants but that's model dependent. 
[06:36] Oliver Price: Any stories on hallucinations with long context? We see drift in summaries when the thread is very long.
[06:41] Ethan Cho: Hallucination increases with context length in naive runs. We mitigate with chunked RAG, retrieval + citation, and credit assignment heuristics. For very long threads we generate summaries in segments then canonicalize. We'll show an eval example in the model perf doc.
[06:58] Maya Singh: Ok. If we decide to pilot, what would be the gating criteria from your side?
[07:03] Sofia Martinez: From Redwood: a PO or pilot agreement, access to sample content, and security questionnaire completion. From your side: a small team to run integration tests and measure business metrics like time-to-resolution and summary accuracy.
[07:16] Oliver Price: Who will be our technical contact at Redwood for the benchmark?
[07:19] Sofia Martinez: Ethan will drive the SE side; I'll own the commercial.
[07:23] Ethan Cho: Yep. I'll set up a benchmarking run and recommend models to test — a small dense LLaMA-3 variant, a Mistral family model, and Falcon-ish for inference cost tradeoff.
[07:34] Maya Singh: Any code or SDKs to make the test easy?
[07:36] Ethan Cho: We have Python and Node SDKs; we'll give you a quickstart notebook that runs your prompt set and captures latency, token counts, and function-call success rates.
[07:45] Priya Nair: On encryption — keys for Private can be customer-managed?
[07:48] Sofia Martinez: Yes, you can bring your own KMS/HSM in Private. For Hosted we offer encrypted-at-rest with Redwood-managed KMS or customer-managed in some enterprise plans.
[07:58] Maya Singh: Anything else we should watch for in terms of model licensing for open weights?
[08:02] Ethan Cho: Good point — model license compatibility is important. We'll flag models with restrictive licenses; for most LLaMA derivatives and community models we note the license and whether commercial use is allowed. That will be in the matrix.
[08:14] Oliver Price: What's the expected latency for 32k context on Dedicated? Tail p99 numbers?
[08:18] Ethan Cho: It depends on model and GPU type. Ballpark: p50 could be sub-second for small batch single requests, p95 for 32k on a single A100-ish node might be several seconds, p99 could be 8–12s depending on quantization and batching. We'll provide precise numbers in the benchmark.
[08:37] Maya Singh: That p99 is acceptable if predictable. The SLA we need is low jitter more than super low median.
[08:44] Sofia Martinez: Understood. Redwood Console can show token-level latency and cost breakdown so you can correlate jitter with model selection.
[08:53] Priya Nair: About legal — will you sign our DPA and addendum for EU data processing?
[08:57] Sofia Martinez: Yes we typically sign DPAs and can include EU data handling addenda. I'll route that to our legal ops.
[09:06] Maya Singh: Okay, let's recap next steps.
[09:09] Sofia Martinez: Recap: Redwood: share model perf matrix and security pack; SE to schedule benchmarking window; customer: share multilingual prompts and long-context examples. We'll also propose pilot commercial terms. Any objections?
[09:22] Oliver Price: No objections.
[09:23] Priya Nair: Sounds good.
[09:25] Maya Singh: Great, thanks everyone.
[09:28] Sofia Martinez: Thanks all — we'll send the notes and the deck.
[09:30] [end meeting]

Notes about transcription quality: a few words mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cash for KV cache, Llama-3 sometimes transcribed as llama three), occasional speaker label confusion at <00:30s>. There are brief crosstalk moments.
